name: Quantitative data assessment
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: online tests for quant research and finance interns at Morgan Stanley and Two Sigma. Statistics and applied maths questions, then Python data tasks.
description: This is the reported format of an online quant assessment, as candidates described it by Nov 2026. It has two papers and takes 120 minutes. The first has 10 statistics and applied maths questions, and some ask you to select all that apply. The second has three Python data tasks that read CSV files. Hidden tests check each task, so run your code before you move on. Use only the standard documentation of the libraries. Use no search engine and no notes.

items.title: An interval for a mean
items.question: 36 daily returns have a sample standard deviation of 12 basis points. Use 1.96 as the multiplier. What is the half-width of a 95% interval for the mean return, in basis points?

feedback.correct: The multiplier applies to the standard error of the mean, $s/\sqrt n$.
feedback.generic: Find the standard error of the mean first. Then scale it by 1.96.

byKey.se-only: You gave the standard error. The interval half-width multiplies it by 1.96.
byKey.no-root-n: You did not divide by $\sqrt n$. The spread of the mean is $12/6$, not 12.

explain.text: The standard error is $12/\sqrt{36} = 2$. The half-width is $1.96 \times 2 = 3.92$ basis points. Check: $1.96\sqrt{144/36}$ gives the same.

items.title: What a p-value says
items.question: A test reports $p = 0.018$ for the average daily profit of a trading rule. What does that mean?

options.text: With a true average profit of zero, results this extreme occur about 1.8% of the time.
There is a 1.8% chance that the rule makes no money at all, given the data.
options.why: You read the p-value as the chance of the hypothesis. It assumes the hypothesis and asks about the data.

options.text: There is a 98.2% chance that the rule makes real money, given the data.
options.why: You turned the p-value into the chance an edge exists. It is not a probability of the hypothesis.

options.text: The rule's average daily profit is 1.8%, which is large enough to trade on.
options.why: You read the p-value as an effect size. It says how surprising the data are, not how big the effect is.

feedback.correct: A p-value assumes the null and asks how surprising the data are.
feedback.generic: Say what the p-value assumes, then what it measures.

explain.text: A p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if the true average were zero. It is not the chance the hypothesis is true, and it gives no effect size. Here, 1.8% is how rare the data would be under no edge.

items.title: A t-statistic
items.question: The mean excess return is 1.8 basis points a day. The sample standard deviation is 5, over 25 days, and the null mean is zero. What is the t-statistic?

feedback.correct: The standard error is $5/\sqrt{25} = 1$, so $t$ is the mean over 1.
feedback.generic: Divide the mean by its standard error, not by the standard deviation.

byKey.wrong-se: You divided by $s/n$, not $s/\sqrt n$. The standard error is 1, not 0.2.
byKey.s-only: You divided by $s$ alone. The mean's own spread is $s/\sqrt n$.

explain.text: The standard error is $5/\sqrt{25} = 1$, so $t = 1.8/1 = 1.8$. Check: $t^2 = n\bar x^2/s^2 = 25 \times 3.24/25 = 3.24$, and $\sqrt{3.24} = 1.8$.

items.title: What always holds in a fit
items.question: Select all that apply: which statements about least squares with an intercept always hold in the sample?

options.text: The fitted line passes through the point of the means.
$R^2$ cannot fall when a predictor is added.

options.why: You treated an assumption about errors as a fact of the fit. Residuals can take any shape.

options.text: The slope's t-test is valid whatever the errors are.
options.why: You dropped the assumptions. The usual t-test needs errors that are roughly independent and equal in spread.

options.text: Adjusted $R^2$ cannot fall when a predictor is added.
options.why: You gave adjusted $R^2$ the property of $R^2$. Its penalty for a predictor can outweigh a small gain.

feedback.correct: Those three follow from the normal equations. The others need assumptions or are false.
feedback.generic: Ask which statements are algebra of the fit and which need assumptions about the errors.

explain.text: The normal equations force the residuals to sum to zero and the line through the means. Adding a column can only lower the sum of squared residuals, so $R^2$ cannot fall. Adjusted $R^2$ charges for the column, so it can fall.

items.title: Adjusted R squared
items.question: A regression has 50 observations and 4 predictors, plus an intercept. $R^2$ is 0.40. What is the adjusted $R^2$? Give four decimals.

feedback.generic: Scale the unexplained share $1 - R^2$ by $(n-1)/(n-k-1)$.

byKey.raw-r2: You gave the reported $R^2$. Adjusting for 4 predictors lowers it.
byKey.n-minus-k: You used $n - k$. With an intercept the divisor is $n - k - 1 = 45$.

items.title: Y given X
items.prose: $X$ has mean 1 and standard deviation 3. $Y$ has mean 4 and standard deviation 2. They are jointly normal with correlation 0.6.

feedback.correct: The slope of $Y$ on $X$ is $\rho\sigma_y/\sigma_x = 0.4$, and $X$ is 4 above its mean.
feedback.generic: Move the mean of $Y$ along the regression line of $Y$ on $X$.

byKey.unconditional: You gave the mean of $Y$. Knowing $X = 5$ moves it along the regression line.
byKey.rho-slope: You used 0.6 as the slope. The slope is $\rho\sigma_y/\sigma_x = 0.4$.

explain.text: The conditional mean is $4 + 0.6 \times (2/3) \times (5 - 1) = 5.6$. Check: $\mu_y + \Sigma_{yx}\Sigma_{xx}^{-1}(x - \mu_x)$ with $\Sigma_{yx} = 3.6$ and $\Sigma_{xx} = 9$ gives the same.

parts.question: What is the standard deviation of $Y$ given $X = 5$?

feedback.generic: The spread left over after $X$ is known depends on $\rho$ but not on the value of $X$.

byKey.unconditional: You gave the spread of $Y$ with $X$ unknown. Knowing $X$ shrinks it by $\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$.
byKey.rho-sigma: You gave $\rho\sigma_y$, the spread that $X$ explains. The leftover is $\sigma_y\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$.

explain.text: The conditional variance is $4(1 - 0.36) = 2.56$, so the standard deviation is 1.6. Check: $\Sigma_{yy} - \Sigma_{yx}^2/\Sigma_{xx} = 4 - 12.96/9 = 2.56$.

items.title: Two assets together
items.question: Two assets have volatility 20% and 30% a year and correlation $-0.3$. You hold 60% in the first and 40% in the second. What is the portfolio volatility, in %?

feedback.correct: The variance has two squared terms and a covariance term, $w^T \Sigma w$.
feedback.generic: Volatilities do not average. Work with variances and the covariance.

byKey.weighted-vols: You weighted the volatilities. That is correct only when the correlation is 1.
byKey.no-covariance: You left out the covariance term. With correlation $-0.3$ it lowers the variance.

explain.text: The variance is $0.0144 + 0.0144 - 0.00864 = 0.02016$. Its square root is 0.1420, so the volatility is 14.2%. Check: $w^T \Sigma w$ with the covariance matrix gives the same.

items.title: The quietest mix
items.question: Two assets have volatility 25% and 20% and correlation 0.3. The weights sum to 1. What weight in the 25% asset gives the minimum-variance portfolio? Give four decimals.

feedback.correct: The weight is $(\sigma_2^2 - c)/(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2c)$ with covariance $c = 0.015$.
feedback.generic: Set the derivative of the portfolio variance to zero. The covariance must appear.

byKey.inverse-variance: You weighted by inverse variance. That ignores the correlation, which here is 0.3.
byKey.equal: You split the money equally. The 20% asset is steadier, so it earns more than half.

explain.text: With $c = 0.015$, the weight is $(0.04 - 0.015)/(0.0625 + 0.04 - 0.03) = 0.025/0.0725 = 10/29$. That is 0.3448. Check: on a grid in steps of $1/290$, the exact variance is lowest at $100/290$.

items.title: Cross-validating returns
items.question: You cross-validate a return-prediction model. Select all that apply: which choices avoid leakage?

options.text: Train on earlier rows and test on later rows.
Fit the scaler on the training fold only.
Leave a gap between training and test when labels overlap.
Shuffle the rows before splitting them into folds.
options.why: You let later rows into training. A shuffled split tests on days the model has seen around.

options.text: Keep the model with the best test-fold score after many tries.
options.why: You tuned on the test fold, so it became training data for the choice. Its score is now too hopeful.

options.text: Standardise every feature with the whole sample.
options.why: You let the test rows set the mean and spread. That leaks the future into the training rows.

feedback.correct: Each correct choice keeps future rows away from the fit.
feedback.generic: For each choice, ask whether the model sees anything from after the forecast date.

explain.text: A model may use only what was known when the forecast was made. A time-ordered split, a scaler fitted on training rows and a gap for overlapping labels all keep to that. Shuffling, tuning on the test fold and whole-sample scaling let the future in.

items.title: Total size of an hour's trades
items.question: Trades arrive as a Poisson process, 4 an hour. Each size has mean 10 and standard deviation 5, independent of the others and of the count. What is the variance of the total size in an hour?

feedback.correct: Use the law of total variance: $\lambda(\sigma^2 + \mu^2)$.
feedback.generic: The total varies for two reasons: each size varies, and so does the count.

byKey.size-only: You counted only the size variance, $4 \times 25$. The varying count adds $4 \times 100$ more.
byKey.count-only: You counted only the spread from the count, $4 \times 100$. Each trade also has its own size variance, $4 \times 25$.
byKey.mean: You gave the mean of the total. The question asks for its variance.

explain.text: By the law of total variance, the variance of the total is $\lambda(\sigma^2 + \mu^2) = 4 \times (25 + 100) = 500$. The count adds spread through $\mu^2$ as well as the sizes through $\sigma^2$. Check: summing over counts from 0 to 79 gives the same.

items.title: A rolling hedge ratio
items.question: `qd-pair.csv` has daily returns for an asset and the market. Three asset returns were typed as whole percents. A return with size above 0.25 in either column is a data error: drop that row. Then write `windowed_betas(window)`. It returns one least-squares slope of `asset` on `mkt` per window of `window` neighbouring remaining rows. Use date order and full windows only.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def windowed_betas(window):
    """Least-squares slope of asset on mkt in each full window of neighbouring rows."""
    ...
widget.how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests. Each slope is accepted within a relative 1e-9.
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def windowed_betas(window):
    df = pd.read_csv("qd-pair.csv")
    df = df[(df["asset"].abs() <= 0.25) & (df["mkt"].abs() <= 0.25)]
    x = df["mkt"].to_numpy()
    y = df["asset"].to_numpy()
    out = []
    for i in range(len(x) - window + 1):
        xs, ys = x[i:i + window], y[i:i + window]
        out.append(float(np.cov(xs, ys, ddof=1)[0, 1] / np.var(xs, ddof=1)))
    return out

feedback.correct: All nine tests pass: the errors are gone and every window is a full one.
feedback.generic: A hidden test failed. Check both columns for data errors, then count the full windows.

explain.text: A return of 0.31 is a whole percent typed in, so drop the row before windowing. The 517 rows left give 458 windows of 60. Keeping the errors gives 461 windows and a different sum.

items.title: An honest out-of-sample score
items.question: `qd-signal.csv` has two signals and the return of each day. Predict a day's return from the signals of the day before. Write `oos_scores(split)`. Row $t$ has the features of row $t - 1$ and the target `ret` of row $t$, for $t = 1$ to 799. Fit least squares with an intercept on the first `split` of these rows. Return a dict with `coef` (intercept, then the two slopes), `train_r2` and `oos_r2`. The out-of-sample score uses the remaining rows. Its baseline is the training mean of the target.

widget.starter:

import pandas as pd

    """Fit on the first split rows, score on the rest. Return coef, train_r2 and oos_r2."""
    ...
widget.how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests. Each number is accepted within a relative 1e-8.
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def oos_scores(split):
    df = pd.read_csv("qd-signal.csv")
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(df) - 1), df["x1"].to_numpy()[:-1], df["x2"].to_numpy()[:-1]])
    y = df["ret"].to_numpy()[1:]
    Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte = X[:split], y[:split], X[split:], y[split:]
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Xtr, ytr, rcond=None)
    train_r2 = 1 - np.sum((ytr - Xtr @ coef) ** 2) / np.sum((ytr - ytr.mean()) ** 2)
    oos_r2 = 1 - np.sum((yte - Xte @ coef) ** 2) / np.sum((yte - ytr.mean()) ** 2)
    return {"coef": [float(c) for c in coef], "train_r2": float(train_r2), "oos_r2": float(oos_r2)}

feedback.correct: All seven tests pass: the fit saw only the first rows and the score used the training mean.
feedback.generic: A hidden test failed. Check the lag, which rows the fit sees, and the baseline of the out-of-sample score.

explain.text: Lag the features so each row predicts forward. Fit on the first rows only, and score the rest against the training mean. A fit on every row, or a test-set baseline, borrows from the future.
